blocks.label: III
blocks.html:
EXPOSÉ III
\(L\)-functions modulo \(\ell^n\) and modulo \(p\)

In this exposé, I prove a formula analogous to the theorem of the Rapport sur la formule des traces (this volume; cited “Rapport” in what follows) for a coefficient ring \(A\) which is of torsion prime to \(p\), or a field of characteristic \(p\). Essential use will be made of [2].
1 Symmetric tensors

Let \(A\) be a commutative ring. For a list of properties of the functors \(\Gamma^n:(A \text{-modules})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} (A \text{-modules})\), I refer to [2]. Let us recall only that for \(M\) flat (in fact, only the case where \(M\) is projective of finite type is of interest to us), one has
\[ \Gamma^n M = \left(M^{\otimes n}\right)^{S_n} \qquad \text{(symmetric tensors of degree } n \text{).} \]

Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme, \(X^n/S\) the \(n\)-th fibre power of \(X\) and \(\pi\) the projection of \(X^n/S\) onto \((X^n/S)/S_n=\operatorname{Sym}_S^n(X)\) (assumed to exist). If \(\mathscr{G}\) is a sheaf of \(A\)-modules on \(X\), the external tensor product of \(n\) copies of \(\mathscr{G}\); \(\mathscr{G}^{\boxtimes n}\), is an \(S_n\)-equivariant sheaf on \(X^n/S\). We shall have to make use of the external functor \(\Gamma^n\) of [2]. Let us recall only that for \(\mathscr{G}\) a sheaf of flat \(A\)-modules (in fact, only the constructible and flat case is of interest to us), one has
\[ \Gamma_\text{ext}^n(\mathscr{G}) = \left(\pi_*\mathscr{G}^{\boxtimes n}\right)^{S_n} \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.3

For \(S=\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), with \(k\) algebraically closed, \(X\) a finite sum of copies of \(S\), and \(G\) a flat sheaf of \(A\)-modules on \(X\), one has

\[ \Gamma\left(\operatorname{Sym}_S^n(X),\Gamma_\text{ext}(\mathscr{G})\right) = \Gamma^n \Gamma(X,\mathscr{G}) \]
Indeed,

\begin{align*} \Gamma\left(\operatorname{Sym}_S^n(X),\Gamma_\text{ext}^n(\mathscr{G})\right) &= \Gamma\left(\operatorname{Sym}_S^n(X),\pi_*\mathscr{G}^{\boxtimes n}\right)^{S_n} \\ &= \Gamma\left(X^n/S,\mathscr{G}^{\boxtimes n}\right)^{S_n} = \left(\Gamma(X,\mathscr{G})^{\otimes n}\right)^{S_n} = \Gamma^n \Gamma(X,\mathscr{G}) \text{.} \end{align*}
We shall have to use the derived functors of the non-additive functors \(\Gamma^n\) and \(\Gamma_\text{ext}^n\).
The theory of these derived functors is due to Dold and Puppe [17]. For more complete reminders than those given below, I refer to [2].

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be an abelian category (or even an additive category in which every idempotent endomorphism is the projection onto a direct summand). Denote by \(N\) the normalization functor: \(N:(\)cosimplicial complexes of objects of \(\mathscr{A})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}(\)differential complexes of objects of \(\mathscr{A}\), with \(K^i\) for \(i<0)\). It is an equivalence of categories. Together with its inverse, it transforms homotopic morphisms into homotopic morphisms. If \(\Gamma\) is a functor \(\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{B}\), and if \(K\) is a complex of objects of \(\mathscr{A}\), in positive degrees (\(K^i=0\) for \(i<0\)), one sets \(T K=N T N^{-1} K\).
1.5 Example
If \(K\) reduces to \(M\) in degree \(0\), then \(T K\) reduces to \(T M\) in degree \(0\).
If \(K\) is a bounded complex, in positive degrees, of projective \(A\)-modules of finite type, the complex of \(A\)-modules \(\Gamma^n K\) has the same properties.

Denote by \(\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}^{\geqslant 0}(A)\) the subcategory of \(\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(A)\) (Rapport, 4.3) formed by the complexes of tor-dimension \(\leqslant 0\). One sees that \(\Gamma^n\) induces a functor
\[ \mathsf{L}\Gamma^n : \mathsf{D}_\text{parf}^{\geqslant 0}(A) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}_\text{parf}^{\geqslant 0}(A) \text{.} \]
For the analogous, but more complicated, definition of \(\mathsf{L}\Gamma_\text{ext}^n\), I refer to [2].
Let \(K\) be a bounded complex of projective \(A\)-modules of finite type, and \(u\) an endomorphism of \(K\). One denotes by \(\det(1-u t,K)\) the formal power series with constant term \(1\)
\[ \det(1-u t,K) = \prod_i \det(1-u t,K^i)^{(-1)^i} \text{.} \]
We leave the verification of the following properties to the reader.
Let \(F\) be a finite filtration stable under \(u\), such that the \(\operatorname{gr}_F^p(K^q)\) are projective of finite type. Then
\[ \det(1-u t,K) = \prod_p \det(1-u t,\operatorname{gr}_F^p(K)) \text{.} \]
If one shifts \(K\) by \(q\) steps to the left, one has
\[ \det(1-u t,K[q]) = \det(1-u t,K)^{(-1)^q} \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.8

Let \(u\) be an endomorphism of a bounded complex, in positive degrees, of \(A\)-modules projective of finite type. One has

\[ \tag{1.8.1} \det(1-u t,K)^{-1} = \sum_n \operatorname{tr}(u,\Gamma^n K) t^n \text{.} \]
Denote by \(D(u,K)\) the right-hand side of (1.8.1).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.9

Let \(u\) be an endomorphism of a short exact sequence of bounded complexes in degrees \(\geqslant 0\) of projective \(A\)-modules of finite type

\[ 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K'' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0 \text{.} \]

One has \(D(u,K)=D(u,K')\cdot D(u,K'')\).

If \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M''\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) is a splittable short exact sequence of \(A\)-modules, \(\Gamma^n M\) has a natural filtration, whose successive quotients are the \(\Gamma^i M'\otimes \Gamma^j M''\) (\(i+j=n\)). Consequently, \(\Gamma^n K\) admits a natural filtration, whose successive quotients are the complexes \(N(N^{-1} \Gamma^i K'\otimes N^{-1}\Gamma^j K'')\) (\(i+j=n\)), canonically homotopic to the simple complexes \(s(\Gamma^i K'\otimes \Gamma^i K'')\) deduced from the double complexes \(\Gamma^i K'\otimes \Gamma^i K''\), and
\[ \operatorname{tr}(u,\Gamma^n K) = \sum_{i+j=n} \operatorname{tr}(u,\Gamma^i K')\cdot \operatorname{tr}(u,\Gamma^j K'') \text{,} \]
whence the lemma. From 1.9, one obtains by induction.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.10

Let \(F\) be a finite filtration of \(K\) stable under \(u\), such that the \(\operatorname{gr}_F^p(K^q)\) are projective of finite type. Then,

\[ D(u,K) = \prod_p D\left(u,\operatorname{gr}_F^p(K)\right) \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.11

Let \(u\) be an endomorphism of a projective \(A\)-module of finite type \(M\), and \(M[-q]\) the complex reduced to \(M\) in degree \(q\). One has

\[ D\left(u,M[-q]\right) = \left(\sum \operatorname{tr}(u,\Gamma^n M) t^n\right)^{(-1)^q} \qquad \text{(} q\geqslant 0 \text{.)} \]
By 1.5, it is true for \(q=0\). Proceeding by induction, it remains to show that
\[ D\left(u,M[-q]\right) \cdot D\left(u,M[-(q+1)]\right) = 1 \text{.} \]
This formula results from 1.9, applied to the complex \(K\) reduced to \(M\) in degrees \(q\) and \(q+1\) (with \(d=\operatorname{id}\)), and to its stupid filtration:

\[ (\cdots 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M \cdots) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} (\cdots M \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} (\cdots M \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0 \cdots) \text{.} \]
Indeed, \(K\) is homotopic to \(0\). In the derived category, one therefore has \(\Gamma^n(K)=\Gamma^n(0)\); \(0\) for \(n>0\) and \(A\) for \(n=0\), and \(D(u,K)=1\).
Let us prove 1.8. By 1.10 applied to the “stupid” filtration of \(K\) by the subcomplexes

\[ 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \cdots \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K^q \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K^{q+1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \cdots \text{,} \]
one has
\[ D(u,K) = \prod_q D\left(u,K^q[-q]\right) =_{\text{(1.10)}} \prod_q \left(\sum \operatorname{tr}\left(u,\Gamma^n(K^q)\right) t^n \right)^{(-1)^q} \text{.} \]
It remains to prove that for \(u\) an endomorphism of a projective module of finite type \(M\), one has
\[ \tag{1.12.1} \det\left(1-u t,M\right)^{-1} = \sum \operatorname{tr}(u,\Gamma^n M) t^n \text{.} \]

If \(u=0\), both sides are equal to \(1\). Adding to \(M\) a module \(N\) on which \(u=0\), and applying 1.9, one reduces to assuming that \(M\) is free. Let us take a basis of it. It is then a matter of proving algebraic identities among the coordinates of \(u\). The principle of extension of algebraic identities reduces us to assuming that \(A\) is an algebraically closed field. The module \(M\) then admits a filtration stable under \(u\) with successive quotients of rank \(1\), and 1.10 reduces us to the case where \(M\) is of rank \(1\). The formula (1.12.1) then reduces to the identity
\[ \frac{1}{1-a t} = \sum a^n t^n \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.13

Let \(u\) and \(u'\) be endomorphisms of bounded complexes \(K\) and \(K'\) of \(A\)-modules projective of finite type. If, in the derived category, \(K\), equipped with \(u\), is isomorphic to \(K'\), equipped with \(u'\), then

\[ \det(1-u t,K) = \det(1-u' t,K') \text{.} \]
Applying 1.7.2, one reduces to assuming that \(K\) and \(K'\) are in positive degrees. One then observes that the right-hand side of 1.8 possesses the desired invariance property.

This corollary allows one to define \(\det(1-u t,K)\) for \(u\) an endomorphism of \(K\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(A)\). This construction is ad hoc; in fact, for \(v\) an automorphism of \(L\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\), one can define \(\det(v)\in\Lambda^\times\), and \(\det(1-u t,K)\) is obtained by taking \(v=1-u t\), \(\Lambda=A[\![ t]\!]\) and \(L=K\otimes_A\Lambda\).
2 The Theorem

Let us resume the notations of (Rapport, §1). For \(A\) a noetherian commutative torsion ring, \(X_0\) a separated scheme of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) and \(\mathscr{K}_0\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{ctf}(X_0;A)\), one sets
\[ L(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = \prod_{x\in |X_0|} \det\left(1-F_x^* t^{\deg(x)}, \mathscr{K}\right)^{-1} \]
(1.7, 1.13 and Rapport, 1.5, 1.6).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.2

In each of the two following cases

  1. \(A\) is of torsion prime to \(p\);

  2. \(A\) is reduced and of characteristic \(p\)

one has

\[ \tag{2.2.1} L(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = \det\left(1-F^* t^f, \mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K})\right)^{-1} \text{.} \]
2.3 Remark

In case a), the method of Rapport, §3 allows one to deduce from the trace formula (Rapport 4.10) that the logarithmic derivatives of the two sides of (2.2.1) are equal. Since the ring \(A\) is torsion, this does not suffice to prove 2.2.
2.4 Remark
If \(A\) is a field, one has
\[ L(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = \prod_i L\left(X_0,\underline{\underline{\operatorname{H}}}^i(\mathscr{K}_0)\right)^{(-1)^i} \]

and the spectral sequence \(E_2^{p q} = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^p(X,\underline{\underline{\operatorname{H}}}^q(\mathscr{K}))\Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{p+q}(X,\mathscr{K})\) shows that

\begin{align*} \det\left(1-F^* t^f, \mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K})\right) &= \prod_n \det\left(1-F^* t^f,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^n(X,\mathscr{K})\right)^{(-1)^n} \\ &= \prod_{p,q} \det\left(1-F^* t^f,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^p(X,\underline{\underline{\operatorname{H}}}^q(\mathscr{K}))\right)^{(-1)^{p+q}} \text{.} \end{align*}
This reduces 2.2 (for \(A\) a field) to the following special case.
If \(\mathscr{G}_0\) is a constructible sheaf of \(A\)-vector spaces, one has
\[ L(X_0,\mathscr{G}_0) = \prod_n \det\left(1-F^* t^f,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^n(X,\mathscr{G})\right)^{(-1)^{n+1}} \text{.} \]
2.5 Remark
It is easy to reduce case b) to the case where \(A\) is a field (or even a finite field) of characteristic \(p\), cf. 4.2.
2.6 Remark
The special case of b) where \(A=\mathbb{Z}/p\), and where \(\mathscr{K}\) is the constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}/p\) concentrated in degree \(0\);
\[ Z(X_0,t) = \prod_{x\in |X_0|} \left(1-t^{\deg(x)}\right)^{-1} \equiv \prod_n \det\left(1-F^* t^f,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^n(X,\mathbb{Z}/p)\right)^{(-1)^{n+1}} \pmod p \]
had been proved by N. Katz [16]. His method, quite different from the one followed here, starts from Dwork's \(p\)-adic theory of \(Z(X_0,t)\).
2.7 Remark
Contrary to what I had imprudently asserted to some friends, one cannot in b) omit the hypothesis “\(A\) reduced.” For a counterexample, cf. 4.5.
2.8 Plan of the proof of 2.2

A shift on the degrees 1.7.2 reduces us to assuming that \(\mathscr{K}_0\) is a bounded complex, in positive degrees, of constructible and flat sheaves of \(A\)-modules. One then has \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K})\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}^{\geqslant 0}(A)\) (Rapport, proof 4.9, b). We shall use 1.8 to expand the two sides of (2.2.1) as power series in \(T=t^f\). The equality of the coefficients of \(T^n\) will follow from [2] and from a trace formula on \(\operatorname{Sym}^n(X)\); in case a), the formula (Rapport, 4.10), and in case b) a formula which will be proved in the following chapter. It is appropriate first to reduce to the case where the symmetric powers of \(X_0\) exist (for example to the case where \(X\) is affine) by means of the multiplicativity properties in \(X_0\) of the two sides of (2.2.1): for \(U_0\) an open subset of \(X_0\), with closed complement \(Y_0\), one has \(L(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0)=L(U_0,\mathscr{K}_0)\cdot L(Y_0,\mathscr{K}_0)\) and the analogous formula for the right-hand side results from 1.7.1 by the method of (Rapport §6A).
2.9 The case where \(X_0\) is finite

The multiplicativity in \(X_0\) of the two sides of (2.2.1) reduces this case to the one where \(X_0=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{F}_{q^k})\). Returning to the definitions, one sees that (2.2.1) is then equivalent to Rapport 3.4.
2.10 The left-hand side
By 1.8, one has
\[ L(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = \prod_{x\in |X_0|} \sum_n \operatorname{tr}\left(F_x^*,\Gamma^n\mathscr{K}\right) t^{n\deg(x)} \text{.} \]

The coefficient of \(T^n\) is therefore the sum, extended over those formal linear combinations \(\sum_{x\in |X_0|} n_x\cdot x\) (\(n_x\geqslant 0\), the \(n_x\) almost all zero) of elements of \(|X_0|\) such that \(\sum n_x [k(x):\mathbb{F}_q] = n\), of the products
\[ \tag{2.10.1} \prod_x \operatorname{tr}\left(F_x^*,\Gamma^{n_x} \mathscr{K}\right) \text{.} \]

For \(x\in |X_0|\), denote by \((x)\) the \(0\)-cycle of the \([k(x):\mathbb{F}_q]\) points of \(X\) above \(x\) (an orbit of \(F\)). The map \(\sum n_x\mapsto \sum n_x\cdot (x)\) identifies the formal linear combinations as above, with \(\sum n_x [k(x):\mathbb{F}_q]=n\), with the effective \(0\)-cycles of degree \(n\) of \(X\) fixed under \(F\), that is, with the fixed points of \(F\) in \(\operatorname{Sym}^n(X)\). The coefficient of \(T^n\) in \(L(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0)\) thus appears as a sum of products (2.10.1), indexed by \(\operatorname{Sym}^n(X)^F\). More precisely,

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.11

\(L(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = \sum_n \sum_{x\in\operatorname{Sym}^n(X)^F} \operatorname{tr}\left(F_x^*,\mathsf{L}\Gamma_\textnormal{ext}^n \mathscr{K}\right) T^n\).
For \(Y_0\) an increasingly large finite subscheme of \(X_0\), one has
\[ L(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = \lim L(Y_0,\mathscr{K}_0) \text{,} \]

i.e., for every \(m\), there exists a finite subscheme \(Z_0\subset X_0\) such that if \(Y_0\supset Z_0\), \(L(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0)\) and \(L(Y_0,\mathscr{K}_0|Y_0)\) are congruent \(\mod T^m\). It suffices that \(Z_0\) contain the closed points of degree \(\leqslant m\). The same fact holding for the right-hand side, it suffices to prove 2.11 for \(X_0\) finite. One then has

\begin{align*} L(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) &=_\text{2.9} \det\left(1-F^* T,\Gamma(X,\mathscr{K})\right)^{-1} \\ &=_\text{1.8} \sum_n \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\Gamma^n \Gamma(X,\mathscr{K})\right) T^n \\ &=_\text{1.3} \sum_n \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\Gamma(\operatorname{Sym}^n(X),\Gamma_\text{ext}^n(\mathscr{K})\right) T^n \\ &= \sum_n \sum_{x\in \operatorname{Sym}^n(X)^F} \operatorname{tr}\left(F_x^*,\Gamma_\text{ext}^n(\mathscr{K})\right) T^n \end{align*}
(by the trace formula in the trivial case of a finite set).
2.12 The right-hand side
By 1.8 and [2], one has

\begin{align*} \det\left(1-F^* T,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K})\right)^{-1} &= \sum_n \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{L}\Gamma^n\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K})\right) T^n \\ &= \sum_n \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(\operatorname{Sym}^n(X),\Gamma_\text{ext}^n\mathscr{K})\right) T^n \text{.} \end{align*}
The theorem is therefore equivalent to the trace formulas

\[ \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(\operatorname{Sym}^n(X,\Gamma_\text{ext}^n \mathscr{K})\right) = \sum_{x\in\operatorname{Sym}^n(X)^F} \operatorname{tr}\left(F_x^*,\Gamma_\text{ext}^n\mathscr{K}\right) \text{.} \]
In case a), they result from Rapport 4.10. The analogous formula in case b) will be proved in §4.
3 Artin-Scheier theory

In what follows, a coherent sheaf on a scheme \(S\) will always be regarded as a sheaf on \(S_\text{ét}\). Let \(S\) be a scheme of characteristic \(p>0\). If \(G\) is a locally constant sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/p\)-vector spaces of finite rank, \(\mathscr{G}=G\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\mathscr{O}\) is a locally free coherent sheaf on \(S\). One will denote by \(\Phi\) both the endomorphism \(f\mapsto f^p\) of \(\mathscr{O}\) and its tensor product with the identity of \(G\): \(\phi:\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}\). Artin-Scheier theory [2] asserts that the sequence
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathbb{Z}/p \ar[r] & \mathscr{O} \ar[r]^-{\Phi-1} & \mathscr{O} \ar[r] & 0 } \]
is exact. By tensoring with \(G\), one finds an exact sequence
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & G \ar[r] & \mathscr{G} \ar[r]^-{\Phi-1} & \mathscr{G} \ar[r] & 0 } \]

Suppose that \(S\) is an open subset in a noetherian scheme \(\overline{S}\). Let \(j:S\hookrightarrow \overline{S}\) be the inclusion morphism, and \(I\) a sheaf of ideals which defines the complementary closed set \(\overline{S}\setminus S\). Denote again by \(\Phi\) the extension by functoriality of \(\Phi\) to \(j_*\mathscr{G}\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.3

There exist coherent extensions \(\overline{\mathscr{G}}\subset j_*\mathscr{G}\) of \(\mathscr{G}\) such that

\[ \tag{3.3.1} \Phi(\overline{\mathscr{G}})\subset I\cdot \overline{\mathscr{G}}\text{.} \]

If \(\overline{\mathscr{G}}\) is such an extension, the sequence

\[ \tag{3.3.2} \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & j_! G \ar[r] & \overline{\mathscr{G}} \ar[r]^-{\Phi-1} & \overline{\mathscr{G}} \ar[r] & 0 } \]

is exact.

1. Existence: Let \(\mathscr{G}'\subset j_*\mathscr{G}\) be a coherent extension of \(\mathscr{G}\) to \(\overline{S}\). For every \(n\), one has \(\Phi(I^n \mathscr{G}')\subset I^{p^n}\Phi(\mathscr{G}')\). Let \(n\) be large enough that \(I^{n(p-1)-1}\Phi(\mathscr{G}')\subset \mathscr{G}'\), and set \(\overline{\mathscr{G}}=I^n\mathscr{G}'\). One has \(\Phi(\overline{\mathscr{G}})\subset I^{p n}\Phi(\mathscr{G}') =I\cdot I^n\cdot I^{n(p-1)-1}\Phi(\mathscr{G}')\subset I\cdot I^n\mathscr{G}' = I\overline{\mathscr{G}}\).

  2. Kernel of \(\Phi-1\): On \(S\), the assertion results from 3.1; it remains to verify that a section \(x\) of \(\ker(\Phi-1)\), on \(U\) étale over \(\overline{S}\), vanishes in a neighbourhood of the inverse image of \(\overline{S}\setminus S\). Since \(x=\Phi(x)\), one indeed has by (3.3.1) \(x\in I\overline{\mathscr{G}}\); moreover, \(x\in I^n\overline{\mathscr{G}}\Rightarrow x=\Phi(x)\in\Phi(I^n\overline{\mathscr{G}})\subset I^{n p}\overline{\mathscr{G}}\), and \(x\) is in all the \(I^n\overline{\mathscr{G}}\), hence zero in the neighbourhood of \(\overline{S}\setminus S\).

  3. Surjectivity of \(\Phi-1\): One may assume \(\overline{S}\) affine, and write \(\mathscr{G}\) as a quotient of \(\mathscr{O}^n\); \(\Phi\) then lifts to a \(p\)-linear map \(\widetilde{\Phi}:\mathscr{O}^n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{O}^n\), and it suffices to verify the surjectivity of \(\widetilde{\Phi}-1\):

    \[ \xymatrix{ \mathscr{O}^n \ar[r]^-{\widetilde{\Phi}-1} \ar[d] & \mathscr{O}^n \ar[d] \\ \mathscr{G} \ar[r]^-{\Phi-1} & \mathscr{G} } \]

    The sheaf \(\mathscr{O}^n\) is the sheaf of local sections of the group scheme \(\mathbb{G}_a^n\), and \(\widetilde{\Phi}-1\) is induced by a homomorphism from \(\mathbb{G}_a^n\) into \(\mathbb{G}_a^n\). This homomorphism is étale. To verify that it is surjective, it suffices to see it after any base change \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\overline{S}\) (\(k\) algebraically closed), and over \(k\) algebraically closed, every étale homomorphism between connected groups of the same dimension is surjective. Finally, an étale and surjective morphism of \(\overline{S}\)-schemes induces an epimorphism between the sheaves corresponding on \({\overline{S}}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\).
3.4 Frobenius and Frobenius

The absolute Frobenius morphism \(F_\text{abs}:S\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) is the identity on the topological space underlying \(S\), and \(f\mapsto f^p\) on the structure sheaf. For \(U/S\) étale, one has a canonical isomorphism \(F_\text{abs}^* U=U\): the diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ U \ar[r]^-{F_{\text{abs}}} \ar[d] & S \ar[d] \\ S \ar[r]^-{F_{\text{abs}}} & S } \]

is cartesian. The endomorphism of ringed site \(({\overline{S}}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}},\mathscr{O})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}({\overline{S}}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}},\mathscr{O})\) defined by \(F_\text{abs}\) can therefore be described as follows:

\(F_\text{abs}^*\) is the identity on \({S}_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}\); the homomorphism \(F_\text{abs}^*\mathscr{O}=\mathscr{O}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{O}\) is \(\Phi\).

With this description, for every étale sheaf \(\mathscr{G}\) on \(S\), the Frobenius correspondence \(F_\text{abs}^*\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}\) is the identity.

To give a \(p\)-linear morphism of quasi-coherent sheaves \(u:\mathscr{M}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{N}\) on \(S\) amounts to giving a linear morphism \(u':F_\text{abs}^*\mathscr{M}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{N}\). In particular, with the notations of 3.5, the homomorphism \(\Phi:\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}\) corresponds to \(\Phi':F_\text{abs}^*\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.5

With the notations of 3.4, the diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ F_{\textnormal{abs}}^* G \ar[r] \ar[d] & G \ar[d] \\ F_{\textnormal{abs}}^*\mathscr{G} \ar[r]^-{\Phi'} & \mathscr{G} } \]

is commutative.
It suffices to verify it locally. One may therefore assume \(G\) constant, in which case the lemma is obvious.
The same theory holds for the powers of \(F_\text{abs}\).

Suppose now that \(\overline{S}\) is a scheme over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) (\(q=p^f\)) and, in accordance with the conventions of Rapport §1, let us write \(S_0,\overline{S}_0,G_0,\mathscr{G}_0,\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0\) instead of \(S,\dots\). Lemma 3.5, for \(F_\text{abs}^f:S_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S_0\), gives a commutative diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ F^* G_0 \ar[r] \ar[d] & G_0 \ar[d] \\ F^*\mathscr{G}_0 \ar[r]^-{(\Phi^f)'} & \mathscr{G}_0 }\qquad\text{, then}\qquad \xymatrix{ F^*(j_! G_0) \ar[r] \ar[d] & j_!G_0 \ar[d] \\ F^*\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0 \ar[r]^-{(\Phi^f)'} & \overline{\mathscr{G}}_0 }\text{,} \]
then, by extension of scalars from \(\mathbb{F}_q\) to \(\mathbb{F}\) and passage to cohomology

\[ \xymatrix{ F^*(j_! G) \ar[r]^-{F_*} \ar[d] & j_!G \ar[d] \\ F^*\overline{\mathscr{G}} \ar[r] & \overline{\mathscr{G}} }\qquad\text{and}\qquad \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{S},j_! G) \ar[r]^-{F^*} \ar[d] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{S},j_!G) \ar[d] \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}}) }\text{,} \]

where the second row is obtained by extension of scalars from \(\mathbb{F}_q\) to \(\mathbb{F}\) of the \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-linear endomorphism \(\Phi^f\) of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{S}_0,\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0)\).
Artin-Scheier theory provides a long exact sequence

\[ \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S},j_! G) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}}) \ar[r]^-{\Phi-1} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}}) \ar[r] & \cdots } \]

where \(\Phi\) is the \(p\)-linear extension to \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}})= \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{S}_0,\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0)\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}\) of the \(p\)-linear endomorphism \(\Phi\) of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{S}_0,\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0)\).

If \(\overline{S}_0\) is proper over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}})\) are finite-dimensional and \(\Phi-1\) is surjective (cf. 3.6b). We thus have

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(S,G) = \ker\left(\Phi-1 : \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}})\right) \text{,} \]

and \(F^*\) is induced by the \(\mathbb{F}\)-linear extension to \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S}_0,\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0)\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}\) of the \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-linear endomorphism \(\Phi^f\) of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S}_0,\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0)\).
Applying Lemma 3.8 below, we deduce the identity

\[ \tag{3.7.1} \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(S,G)\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(\Phi^f,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S}_0,\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0)\right) \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.8

Let \(\Phi\) be a \(p\)-linear endomorphism of a vector space \(V\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\): \(\phi(\lambda x) = \lambda^p\phi(x)\). We set \(F=\Phi^f\) (\(F\) is linear) and we again denote by \(\Phi\) and \(F\) the respectively \(p\)-linear extensions of \(\Phi\) and \(F\) to \(V\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}\). Then \(F\) stabilizes \(\ker(\Phi-1)\subset V\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}\) and

\[ \operatorname{tr}\left(F,\ker(\Phi-1)\right) = \operatorname{tr}(F,V) = \operatorname{tr}\left(F,V\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}\right) \text{.} \]

On \(V\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}\), we have \(F\Phi = \Phi F\): the \(p\)-linear endomorphism \(F\Phi-\Phi F\) vanishes on \(V\), hence everywhere. Let us write \(V=V'+V''\), with \(F\) invertible on \(V'\) and nilpotent on \(V''\). The theory of \(p\)-linear endomorphisms ensures that
\[ \ker(\Phi-1)\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F} \xrightarrow{\sim} V'\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F} \text{.} \]
Since \(\operatorname{tr}(F,V'') = 0\), we thus have

\begin{align*} \operatorname{tr}\left(F,\ker(\Phi-1)\right) &= \operatorname{tr}\left(F,\ker(\Phi-1)\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(F,V'\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}\right) \\ &= \operatorname{tr}\left(F,V\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}\right) = \operatorname{tr}(F,V) \text{.} \end{align*}
4 Trace formula modulo \(p\)

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.1

Let \(X_0\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), \(A\) a reduced commutative noetherian ring of characteristic \(p\), and \(\mathscr{K}_0\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\textnormal{ctf}(X_0,A)\). We have

\[ \tag{4.1.1} \sum_{x\in X^F} \operatorname{tr}\left(F_x^*,\mathscr{K}_x\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K})\right) \text{.} \]
4.2 Reduction to the case where \(A\) is a finite field

A standard passage-to-the-limit argument reduces us to the case where \(A\) is of finite type over \(\mathbb{Z}/p\). For each maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) of \(A\), the image of each side of (4.1.1) in \(A/\mathfrak{m}\) is given by the same formula, with \(\mathscr{K}_0\) replaced by \(\mathscr{K}_0\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_A A/\mathfrak{m}\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{ctf}(X_0,A/\mathfrak{m})\) (for the right-hand side, cf. Rapport 4.12). Since the \(A/\mathfrak{m}\) are finite, and the intersection of the maximal ideals of \(A\) reduces to \(0\), we obtain the announced reduction.
4.3 Reduction to the case where \(A=\mathbb{Z}/p\)

Suppose that \(A\) is a finite field, and denote by \(T_A'(\mathscr{K}_0)\) and \(T_A''(\mathscr{K}_0)\) the two sides of (4.1.1). If, by restriction of scalars, we regard \(\mathscr{K}_0\) as a complex of sheaves of \(\mathbb{Z}/p\)-modules, we have
\[ T_{\mathbb{Z}/p}'(\mathscr{K}_0) = \operatorname{tr}_{A/(\mathbb{Z}/p)} T_A'(\mathscr{K}_0) \]
and similarly for \(T''\). If (4.1.1) holds for \(A=\mathbb{Z}/p\), we thus have
\[ \tag{4.3.1} \operatorname{tr}_{A/(\mathbb{Z}/p)} T_A'(\mathscr{K}_0) = \operatorname{tr}_{A/(\mathbb{Z}/p)} T_A''(\mathscr{K}_0) \text{.} \]
I claim that, for all \(\lambda\in A\), we even have
\[ \tag{4.3.2} \operatorname{tr}_{A/(\mathbb{Z}/p)}\left(\lambda\cdot T_A'(\mathscr{K}_0)\right) = \operatorname{tr}_{A/(\mathbb{Z}/p)}\left(\lambda\cdot T_A''(\mathscr{K}_0)\right) \text{,} \]

and therefore \(T_A'(\mathscr{K}_0) = T_A''(\mathscr{K}_0)\). This is clear for \(\lambda=0\). For \(\lambda\) invertible, denote by \(A(\lambda)\) the inverse image on \(X\) of the sheaf of \(A\)-modules, free of rank one, on \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{F}_q)\) for which \(F^*=\lambda\). Formula (4.3.2) is none other than (4.3.1) for \(A(\lambda)\otimes_A \mathscr{K}_0\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.4

Let \(\overline{S}_0\) be a smooth projective curve, \(j:S_0\hookrightarrow \overline{S}_0\) a dense open subset of \(\overline{S}_0\), and \(G_0\) a locally constant sheaf of finite-rank \(\mathbb{Z}/p\)-vector spaces on \(S_0\). We have

\[ \tag{4.4.1} \sum_{x\in S^F} \operatorname{tr}\left(F_x^*,G_x\right) = \sum_i (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(S,G)\right) \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Démonstration
blocks.html:
Proof▾

Let us apply 3.3 to \((S_0,\overline{S}_0,G_0)\). The coherent extension \(\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0\) of \(\mathscr{G}_0\), whose existence 3.3 guarantees, is locally free because it is torsion-free (we have \(\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0\subset j_*\mathscr{G}_0\)) and \(\overline{S}_0\) is regular of dimension one. The \(q\)-linear endomorphism \(\Phi^f\) of \(\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0\) can be interpreted as a morphism

\[ u : F^*\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{\mathscr{G}}_0 \text{.} \]

It factors through \(I\overline{G}\), where \(I\) defines the closed subset \(\overline{S}\setminus S\). Let \(v:j_!G_0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \overline{\mathscr{G}}_0\) be the unique extension of the natural map \(G_0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{G}_0 = G_0\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\mathscr{O}\). The diagram

\[ \tag{4.4.2} \xymatrix{ F^* j_! G_0 \ar[r]^-{F^*} \ar[d]^-{F^* v} & j_! G_0 \ar[d]^-v \\ F^*\overline{\mathscr{G}}_0 \ar[r]^-u & \overline{\mathscr{G}}_0 } \]

Finally, denote by \(u F^*\) the composite map

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}}) \ar[r]^-{F^*} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{S},F^*\overline{\mathscr{G}}) \ar[r]^-u & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}}) , } \]

we have, by (3.7.1),

\[ \tag{4.4.3} \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(S,G)\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(u F^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}})\right) \text{.} \]

For each closed point \(i_x:x\hookrightarrow \overline{S}\) of \(\overline{S}\), set \(\overline{\mathscr{G}}_x = i_x^*\overline{\mathscr{G}}\). The Lefschetz trace formula in coherent cohomology (“Woodshole fixed point formula”), applied to \(F\) and \(u\), says that

\[ \tag{4.4.4} \sum_i (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\left(u^* F^*, \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{S},\overline{\mathscr{G}})\right) = \sum_{x\in \overline{S}^F} \frac{\operatorname{tr}(u_x,\mathscr{G}_x)}{\det(1-d F_x)} \text{.} \]

On the right-hand side

  1. since \(d F=0\), the denominators equal 1;

  2. for \(x\in \overline{S}^F\setminus S^F\), the endomorphism \(u_x\) of \(\overline{\mathscr{G}}_x\) is zero, hence so is \(\operatorname{tr}(u_x,\overline{\mathscr{G}}_x)\);

  3. for \(x\in S^F\), (4.4.4) yields a contribution

    \[ \operatorname{tr}(u_x,\overline{\mathscr{G}}_x) = \operatorname{tr}(F_x^*,G_x) \text{.} \]

    The identity (4.4.1) thus follows from (4.4.3) and (4.4.4).

Q.E.D.
4.5 A counterexample
We show by an example that one cannot, in 4.1, omit the hypothesis that \(A\) be reduced.

Let \(Y_0\) be the elliptic curve over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) for which the eigenvalues of Frobenius are \(\pm \sqrt{-2}\). It has \(3\) rational points, and is supersingular. The involution \(\sigma:x\mapsto -x\) thus has only a single fixed point, the point \(0\). The quotient of \(Y_0\) by \(\sigma\) is a projective line; that of \(Y_0\setminus 0\) by \(\sigma\) is thus an affine line \(\mathbb{F}_0^1\), and \(Y_0\setminus 0\) is an unramified double covering of \(\mathbb{F}_0^1\):
\[ \pi:Y_0\setminus 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{A}_0^1 \qquad \text{, } \pi=\pi\sigma \text{.} \]

The sheaf \(\pi_*\mathbb{Z}/2\) is a free module of rank one over the algebra \(A\) of the two-element group \(\{1,\sigma\}\) over \(\mathbb{Z}/2\). This algebra is isomorphic to that of the numbers over \(\mathbb{Z}/2\).
The sheaf of \(A\)-modules \(\pi_*\mathbb{Z}/2\) is our example:

1. We have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(\mathbb{A}^1,\pi_*\mathbb{Z}/2) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(Y\setminus 0,\mathbb{Z}/2)\). Since \(Y_0\) is supersingular, we have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(Y,\mathbb{Z}/2)=0\) for \(i>0\), and the long exact sequence

    \[ \cdots \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(Y\setminus 0,\mathbb{Z}/2) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(Y,\mathbb{Z}/2) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\{0\},\mathbb{Z}/2) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \cdots \]

    shows that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(Y\setminus 0,\mathbb{Z}/2)=0\). We thus have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(\mathbb{A}^1,\pi_*\mathbb{Z}/2)=0\) and

    \[ \operatorname{tr}_A\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(\mathbb{A}^1,\pi_*\mathbb{Z}/2)\right) = 0 \text{.} \]

  2. Since \(Y_0\setminus 0\) has two rational points, at one of the rational points of \(\mathbb{A}_1^0\), the Frobenius substitution is the identity, and at the other, it is \(\sigma\). We thus have

    \[ \sum_{x\in {\mathbb{A}^1}^F} \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\pi_*\mathbb{Z}/2\right) = 1+\sigma \text{,} \]

    and \(1+\sigma\ne 0\).
The equation of the covering \(\pi\) is \(y^2-y=x^3\).
